deep.lede: Matthew and Luke both open Jesus' great sermon with blessings, almost certainly from a shared source, the hypothetical sayings collection called Q. Yet the two versions are addressed to different people and promise different things. Matthew's are mostly about spiritual dispositions; Luke's are about poverty and hunger, and they come with matching woes.

sections.heading: “Poor” or “poor in spirit”?
sections.body:
Matthew's first beatitude is {mt 5:3 Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι} (“blessed are the poor **in spirit**”). Luke's is {lk 6:20 Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοί} (“blessed are the poor”) with no qualification, and in the second person: {lk 6:20 ὑμετέρα ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ} (“**yours** is the kingdom of God”).

Most scholars think Luke's shorter, direct form is closer to the source, and that Matthew added “in spirit” and “for righteousness” ({mt 5:6 πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν δικαιοσύνην}, “hunger and thirst for righteousness”). The poor (*anawim*) of the Psalms and Isaiah were both materially poor and humbly reliant on God, so Matthew may be bringing out a meaning already present rather than spiritualizing it away. Readers still disagree about whether Matthew's change softens Jesus or clarifies him. Many traditional readers see two different sermons, one on a mountain and one on a level place, since a travelling teacher would repeat his core teaching in different forms.

sections.heading: Luke's “now” and the woes
sections.body:
Luke repeats one small word: {lk 6:21 μακάριοι οἱ πεινῶντες νῦν} (“blessed are you who are hungry **now**”), {lk 6:21 μακάριοι οἱ κλαίοντες νῦν ὅτι γελάσετε} (“who weep now, for you will laugh”). Then he does something Matthew does not: he adds four woes, the reverse of the four blessings. {lk 6:24 οὐαὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις ὅτι ἀπέχετε τὴν παράκλησιν ὑμῶν} (“woe to you who are rich, for you have received your comfort”). The verb *apechō* was a technical term on receipts: “paid in full”.

The pattern of reversal, the hungry filled and the rich sent away empty, runs through Luke from Mary's song (1:53) to the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (16:25).

sections.heading: Nine and four
sections.body: Matthew has nine blessings (or eight, plus a closing one in the second person), and Luke has four. Matthew's extra blessings, for the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart and the peacemakers, have no parallel in Luke. Several echo the Psalms (“the meek shall inherit the land”, Psalm 37:11). Luke's sermon is set {lk 6:17 ἐπὶ τόπου πεδινοῦ} (“on a level place”), Matthew's on a mountain, and the setting matches the content. Matthew's Jesus is a new Moses giving instruction from a height; Luke's stands among the crowd.

deep.lede: The best-known prayer in Christianity survives in two Gospel versions of different lengths, set in different scenes. Matthew places it in the Sermon on the Mount as a model prayer; in Luke a disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray, “as John taught his disciples”. Where the two versions differ, they show early Christian worship taking shape.

sections.heading: Father, and “our Father in heaven”
sections.body:
Luke's prayer begins with one word, {lk 11:2 Πάτερ} (“Father”), probably the Aramaic *abba* that Jesus used in Gethsemane. Matthew's opening is fuller and more liturgical: {mt 6:9 Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς} (“Our Father in heaven”), the way a synagogue prayer would address God. Matthew also has two petitions Luke lacks: {mt 6:10 γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου} (“your will be done”) and {mt 6:13 ἀλλὰ ῥῦσαι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ} (“but deliver us from evil”, or “from the evil one”).

A common rule in textual criticism is that liturgical texts tend to grow rather than shrink. So most scholars think Luke's shorter version is closer to the original wording, and Matthew's reflects how his church prayed it. Luke, however, gives the prayer a different occasion, a disciple's request, and many traditional readers think Jesus taught it more than once. The early church manual known as the Didache (8:2) gives a version almost identical to Matthew's, with a doxology.

sections.heading: A word no one knows
sections.body:
Both Gospels ask for bread that is {mt 6:11 τὸν ἐπιούσιον} / {lk 11:3 τὸν ἐπιούσιον}. The adjective *epiousios* has no secure attestation in Greek before the Gospels, and the third-century scholar Origen thought the evangelists had coined it. It might mean “daily”, “for tomorrow”, “necessary for existence”, or even “supersubstantial” (Jerome's Latin rendering in Matthew). Its presence in both Gospels is strong evidence of a shared written Greek source.

The timing differs too: Matthew asks for bread {mt 6:11 σήμερον} (“today”), Luke {lk 11:3 τὸ καθ ἡμέραν} (“each day”), with a present-tense verb implying an ongoing need.

sections.heading: Debts or sins?
sections.body:
Matthew prays {mt 6:12 ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν} (“forgive us our **debts**”). In Aramaic, the word for debt (*ḥôbâ*) was a common way of speaking of sin, and Matthew's literal rendering keeps it. Luke translates the idea for his readers, {lk 11:4 τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν} (“our **sins**”), but then lets the debt image slip back in: {lk 11:4 ἀφίομεν παντὶ ὀφείλοντι ἡμῖν} (“we forgive everyone **indebted** to us”). Luke's half-finished translation is a small sign that a more Semitic wording lies behind both versions.

The doxology many Christians say, “for yours is the kingdom, the power and the glory”, is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew. It was added from liturgical use, and modern critical editions don't print it.

deep.lede: “Love your enemies” is in both Matthew and Luke, almost word for word: {mt 5:44 ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν} and {lk 6:27 ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν}. Most scholars regard it as one of the sayings most securely traceable to Jesus himself. Around that shared core, Matthew and Luke build different arguments.

sections.heading: Cheeks, cloaks and miles
sections.body:
Matthew frames the teaching as one of his “antitheses”, set against the law of retaliation, “an eye for an eye”. The examples are specific. {mt 5:39 ὅστις σε ῥαπίζει εἰς τὴν δεξιὰν σιαγόνα} (“whoever slaps you on the **right** cheek”) is often taken to imply a backhanded slap, an insult rather than an assault. {mt 5:41 ὅστις σε ἀγγαρεύσει μίλιον ἕν} (“whoever forces you to go one mile”) uses a Persian loanword for compulsory service, such as a Roman soldier's right to make a civilian carry his pack.

Luke has no antithesis and no forced mile. His cloak example is about robbery, not a court case: {lk 6:29 ἀπὸ τοῦ αἴροντός σου τὸ ἱμάτιον} (“from one who takes your cloak”), so the order of garments is reversed. Matthew's tunic is taken by lawsuit and the cloak given as well; Luke's thief snatches the outer garment first.

sections.heading: “What credit is that?”
sections.body: Both Gospels argue that loving only those who love you is nothing special, but each uses different words. Matthew: {mt 5:46 τίνα μισθὸν ἔχετε} (“what **reward** do you have?”), and even {mt 5:46 οἱ τελῶναι} (“the tax collectors”) and {mt 5:47 οἱ ἐθνικοὶ} (“the Gentiles”) do that. Luke: {lk 6:32 ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν} (“what **credit** is that to you?”), and even {lk 6:32 οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ} (“sinners”) do it. Luke's terms would be familiar to Greek readers, since *charis* (favor, credit) was the language of benefaction and reciprocity in the Greco-Roman world. Matthew's examples come from a Jewish community's boundary markers.

sections.heading: Perfect or merciful?
sections.body:
The climax differs strikingly. Matthew: {mt 5:48 Ἔσεσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι ὡς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τέλειός ἐστιν} (“be **perfect**, as your heavenly Father is perfect”). Luke: {lk 6:36 γίνεσθε οἰκτίρμονες καθὼς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν οἰκτίρμων ἐστίν} (“be **merciful**, as your Father is merciful”). Both echo Leviticus 19:2, “be holy, for I am holy”. *Teleios* means “complete” or “whole” more than flawless, so Matthew's demand is for undivided love that matches God's generosity to both just and unjust.

Luke places the Golden Rule here ({lk 6:31 καθὼς θέλετε ἵνα ποιῶσιν ὑμῖν οἱ ἄνθρωποι}); Matthew holds it until near the end of the sermon and adds a summary: {mt 7:12 οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται} (“for this is the Law and the Prophets”).

deep.lede: John the Baptist's sermon is one of the most important passages for the Synoptic problem. Matthew and Luke agree here almost word for word, more than 80% by this site's alignment, in material that Mark does not have. This is the strongest kind of evidence for the shared source scholars call Q, or, on the Farrer view, for Luke copying Matthew.

sections.heading: Sixty identical words
sections.body:
Compare the opening: {mt 3:7 Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν τίς ὑπέδειξεν ὑμῖν φυγεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς} and {lk 3:7 Γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν τίς ὑπέδειξεν ὑμῖν φυγεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς} (“you brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?”). The two are identical down to word order. The warning about Abraham is the same: {mt 3:9 δύναται ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῶν λίθων τούτων ἐγεῖραι τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ} (“God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones”). Oral tradition rarely keeps sentences this long unchanged, so a **written** Greek source is the usual explanation.

Where they do differ, it is in a single verb: Matthew's {mt 3:9 μὴ δόξητε λέγειν} (“do not presume to say”) against Luke's {lk 3:8 μὴ ἄρξησθε λέγειν} (“do not begin to say”).

sections.heading: Who was the audience?
sections.body: The words are the same, but the audience is not. In Matthew, John addresses {mt 3:7 πολλοὺς τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ Σαδδουκαίων} (“many of the Pharisees and Sadducees”); in Luke, {lk 3:7 τοῖς ἐκπορευομένοις ὄχλοις} (“the crowds that came out”). Matthew turns the sermon into an attack on religious leaders, which suits his Gospel's running conflict with the Pharisees. Luke makes it a warning to everyone. Most scholars think Luke's broader audience is closer to the source, since pairing Pharisees with Sadducees is a Matthean habit (it recurs four times in chapter 16).

sections.heading: Luke's practical ethics
sections.body: Luke alone adds a question-and-answer section. The crowds ask {lk 3:10 Τί οὖν ποιήσωμεν} (“what then should we do?”), and John answers concretely: {lk 3:11 Ὁ ἔχων δύο χιτῶνας μεταδότω τῷ μὴ ἔχοντι} (“whoever has two tunics should share with the one who has none”). Tax collectors are told not to over-collect, and soldiers not to extort. It is classic Luke: repentance means economic justice, and the same question recurs in Acts (2:37).

deep.lede: The saying about birds and lilies is one of the most loved passages in the Gospels, and one of the closest matches between Matthew and Luke. Their wording overlaps by over 60%. Their small differences are the kind that reveal two editors working on the same text.

sections.heading: Birds or ravens?
sections.body: Matthew says {mt 6:26 ἐμβλέψατε εἰς τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ} (“look at the **birds** of the air”); Luke says {lk 12:24 κατανοήσατε τοὺς κόρακας} (“consider the **ravens**”). Ravens were unclean under Leviticus 11:15, and a scavenger bird makes a sharper point: God feeds even them. Most scholars think Luke kept the original “ravens” and Matthew generalized it, though Psalm 147:9 (“he gives the beasts their food, and the young ravens that cry”) could have pulled the wording either way. Matthew's God is {mt 6:26 ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος} (“your heavenly Father”), his favorite phrase; Luke's is simply {lk 12:24 ὁ θεὸς} (“God”).

sections.heading: The lilies and Solomon
sections.body: Both share an unforgettable image: the lilies {mt 6:28 οὐ κοπιῶσιν οὐδὲ νήθουσιν} (“neither toil nor spin”), yet not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of them. Then comes the grass, here today and {mt 6:30 αὔριον εἰς κλίβανον βαλλόμενον} (“tomorrow thrown into the oven”), since dried grass was used as fuel. Matthew's address {mt 6:30 ὀλιγόπιστοι} (“you of little faith”) is one of his favorite words for the disciples; he uses it four times, Luke once.

sections.heading: Seek first
sections.body:
Matthew adds two words to the climax: {mt 6:33 ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ} (“seek **first** the kingdom and **his righteousness**”). Luke has {lk 12:31 ζητεῖτε τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτοῦ} (“seek his kingdom”). Righteousness (*dikaiosynē*) is a key word for Matthew, seven times in his Gospel against once in Luke, so most scholars see Matthew's hand here.

Each ends differently. Matthew closes with proverbial realism: {mt 6:34 ἀρκετὸν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἡ κακία αὐτῆς} (“each day has enough trouble of its own”). Luke closes with tenderness: {lk 12:32 Μὴ φοβοῦ τὸ μικρὸν ποίμνιον} (“do not be afraid, little flock”), followed by the promise that the Father is pleased to give them the kingdom.

deep.lede: Asked for a sign, Jesus refuses, except for “the sign of Jonah”. Mark records only the refusal. Matthew and Luke share a longer version, nearly identical, but each explains the sign of Jonah differently, and the difference may reveal a source being interpreted.

sections.heading: Mark's flat refusal
sections.body: Mark's version is short and absolute: {mk 8:12 ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν εἰ δοθήσεται τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον} (“truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation”). The Greek copies a Hebrew oath formula, literally “if a sign will be given…”, with the curse left unspoken. Matthew and Luke agree on a qualification Mark lacks: {mt 12:39 εἰ μὴ τὸ σημεῖον Ἰωνᾶ} (“except the sign of Jonah”), and Luke's {lk 11:29 εἰ μὴ τὸ σημεῖον Ἰωνᾶ}. This is a case of Mark and Q overlapping.

sections.heading: Three days, or a preacher?
sections.body:
What is the sign? Luke: {lk 11:30 καθὼς γὰρ ἐγένετο Ἰωνᾶς τοῖς Νινευίταις σημεῖον} (“as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites”), so the Son of Man will be to this generation. The sign is the preacher himself and his call to repent.

Matthew adds a specific interpretation: {mt 12:40 ὥσπερ γὰρ ἦν Ἰωνᾶς ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ τοῦ κήτους τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας} (“as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster”), so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth. The sign has become the resurrection. Most scholars think Luke's version is closer to the source and Matthew's is a later Christian reading. Traditional readers hold that Jesus himself pointed to both, his preaching and his resurrection; Matthew records the demand for a sign twice (12:38, 16:1). The detail “three nights” fits awkwardly with a burial from Friday to Sunday, which suggests Matthew was quoting Jonah 1:17 rather than counting. In Jewish reckoning, though, part of a day could count as a whole “day and night”, so the phrase need not mean seventy-two hours.

sections.heading: Something greater
sections.body:
Both close with two witnesses against “this generation”, Gentiles who responded when Israel did not. The Queen of the South came to hear Solomon; the men of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching. Each ends with {mt 12:41 ἰδοὺ πλεῖον Ἰωνᾶ ὧδε} (“behold, something greater than Jonah is here”). The adjective is neuter, *pleion*, “something greater”, not “someone”. It may refer to the kingdom breaking in, not only to Jesus himself.

The two Gospels reverse the order. Matthew puts Nineveh first, linking it to his Jonah explanation, and Luke puts the Queen first, which is likely chronological (Solomon before Jonah). These small rearrangements are typical of how each evangelist edits shared material.

deep.lede: A host invites guests to a great feast; they refuse; he fills the hall with others. Matthew and Luke both tell this parable, but they share only about 15% of its wording, so low that some scholars doubt they had a common written source here. Matthew's version especially has been transformed into an allegory of history.

sections.heading: Luke: excuses and outcasts
sections.body: Luke's version is a realistic story of social insult. {lk 14:16 Ἄνθρωπός τις ἐποίει δεῖπνον μέγα} (“a certain man was giving a great dinner”), and the guests {lk 14:18 ἤρξαντο ἀπὸ μιᾶς πάντες παραιτεῖσθαι} (“all alike began to make excuses”): a field, oxen, a marriage. The angry host sends his servant to bring {lk 14:21 τοὺς πτωχοὺς καὶ ἀναπείρους καὶ τυφλοὺς καὶ χωλοὺς} (“the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame”). They are the same four groups Jesus had told his own host to invite, eight verses earlier (14:13). Then there is a second sending, to the roads and hedges outside the city: {lk 14:23 ἀνάγκασον εἰσελθεῖν} (“compel them to come in”). Augustine later used this phrase to justify coercing heretics.

sections.heading: Matthew: a king, a war, a burned city
sections.body:
Matthew's host is {mt 22:2 ἀνθρώπῳ βασιλεῖ ὅστις ἐποίησεν γάμους τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ} (“a king who gave a wedding feast for his son”). The invited guests do not just make excuses: some {mt 22:6 ἀπέκτειναν} (“killed”) the servants. The king {mt 22:7 πέμψας τὰ στρατεύματα αὐτοῦ ἀπώλεσεν τοὺς φονεῖς ἐκείνους καὶ τὴν πόλιν αὐτῶν ἐνέπρησεν} (“sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city”), all while the dinner is waiting.

The story has broken its own frame. Most scholars read verse 7 as an allusion to the Roman burning of Jerusalem in 70 CE, which would mean Matthew wrote after that date. Those who date Matthew earlier read it as prophecy, or as a stock image of a king punishing rebels, and many traditional readers think Jesus told two different parables. The king is God, the son is Jesus, the murdered servants are the prophets, much as in the parable of the wicked tenants just before it.

sections.heading: The wedding garment
sections.body:
Matthew adds a second scene with no parallel in Luke. The servants gather {mt 22:10 πονηρούς τε καὶ ἀγαθούς} (“both bad and good”), and the king finds a man {mt 22:11 οὐκ ἐνδεδυμένον ἔνδυμα γάμου} (“not wearing a wedding garment”), who is bound and thrown {mt 22:13 εἰς τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον} (“into the outer darkness”). Matthew's church was itself a mixed body. The open invitation does not end with entry, and the final line warns the insiders: {mt 22:14 πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοὶ ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί} (“many are called, but few are chosen”).

A third version survives in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 64), where the excuses are commercial and the conclusion attacks merchants. That makes it a useful independent test of what the parable's original form may have been.
